## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure commits an unusually large and concentrated pool of capital: combined 2026 capital expenditure by the four largest compute providers was guided to roughly \$720--745 billion in mid-2026, up from \$660--690 billion at the start of the year,^[Sources: Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings release (SEC EDGAR, exhibit 99.1, July 22, 2026); Meta Q2 2026 earnings release (July 29, 2026); Amazon and Microsoft Q2 2026 earnings calls (July 29--30, 2026), as reported by CNBC and CFO Dive.] OpenAI's Stargate joint venture targets up to \$500 billion in U.S. AI infrastructure through 2029,^[\url{https://openai.com/index/announcing-the-stargate-project/}.] and Anthropic's forward compute commitments reportedly exceed \$500 billion, most of them non-cancellable.^[Reuters, reporting on Anthropic's IPO prospectus, September 28, 2026.] These investments are largely irreversible, and whether and when AI capabilities will reach a transformative threshold, the uncertainty that drives them, remains unresolved. This paper asks how a firm should time, size, and allocate an irreversible capacity investment when the return to that capacity depends on a regime change whose arrival is uncertain and whose competitive consequences depend on how the capacity was used beforehand.

The allocation margin is what makes the problem distinctive. A frontier AI laboratory produces intelligence by combining two forms of compute drawn from the same scarce hardware: *training compute*, which optimizes a neural network's parameters on massive datasets and yields a model whose quality scales as a power law of compute invested [@kaplan2020scaling; @altman2025observations], and *inference compute*, which runs the trained model to serve predictions and generate revenue. The same asset can either produce revenue now or build the capability that determines the firm's position in a future that may not arrive. Capacity devoted to training earns nothing until that future arrives, while its operating cost is paid from the start. The split therefore sets both what the firm is worth if the switch comes and how far demand can fall before the firm stops operating, so the option to grow and the risk of failure run through a single decision.

Firms must commit this capital under widely different priors about the same event. The prize is Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): a step change in model capability sufficient to automate a broad range of cognitive tasks and generate sustained, qualitatively higher demand for compute [@amodei2024machines]. Executive forecasts of its arrival run from "superintelligence in a few thousand days" [@altman2024intelligence] and 2026--2027 [@amodei2024machines], through "AGI in 2026,"^[Elon Musk, post on X, 2026: \url{https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2025124840806514916}.] to "not with current architectures."^[PYMNTS, "Meta: Large Language Models Will Not Get to Human-Level Intelligence," 2025.]

Existing frameworks illuminate parts of this problem but not its core difficulty. Real-options models [@mcdonald1986value; @dixit1994investment] characterize irreversibility and timing but take the use of installed capacity as given; R&D race models [@loury1979market; @reinganum1982strategic] treat pre-breakthrough expenditure as pure cost with no concurrent revenue; structural credit models [@leland1994corporate], including the branch that embeds regime switching, take the size of the growth option as exogenous rather than as a capacity-allocation choice.

I therefore develop a model in which a firm chooses when to invest, how much capacity to install, and what fraction $\phi$ to devote to training versus inference, facing regime-switching demand [@guo2005investment], a rival in a duopoly timing game [@grenadier2002option; @huisman2015strategic], endogenous default [@leland1994corporate], and diminishing returns to capacity, with the curvature parameter motivated by empirical scaling laws [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training]. In regime $L$, the current low-demand regime, revenue depends on inference capacity through a Tullock contest, in which a firm's contest share is its inference capacity's share of the industry total, each raised to the power $\alpha$; in regime $H$, the post-AGI regime, it depends on training compute. A firm may invest before or after the switch, and I solve its problem in these primitives: the allocation and the post-switch policy in closed form, the pre-switch policy and the duopoly equilibrium numerically. Duopoly is the minimal setting in which entry timing, the allocation, and leverage interact with a rival's capacity.

The paper makes three contributions. First, I find that in the calibrated model competition, and not the single firm's own option, is what brings investment forward of the switch. The optimal training fraction has a closed form that rises with the arrival rate of the switch and does not depend on scale, so it is the allocation of any investment made before the switch (Proposition 1). Timing and scale have no such property. At the baseline calibration a single firm that can choose its scale when the switch arrives waits for it, because investing earlier buys only pre-switch inference revenue while the post-switch prize is obtained at least as cheaply by waiting; a finite pre-switch trigger exists only for arrival rates below about $0.073$. In the duopoly one firm invests before the switch at every arrival rate examined (Proposition 3). The force at work is the race that follows the switch and not a race before it: a firm that waits enters a post-switch contest in which the rent from leading is competed away, and installing early secures a position ahead of it. At the date of first investment following is the better role, so the pre-switch game has a second-mover advantage, and the demand level at which leading and following are worth the same is an upper bound on that date. Against a single firm whose post-switch scale is precommitted, which always has a finite trigger, first investment comes at a demand level $64\%$ lower at baseline. Competitive position moves the allocation only modestly: against a rival with the same training fraction the contest shares drop out of the allocation condition, and in equilibrium the leader's training fraction lies $3.1\%$ below the single firm's at baseline, while a follower that enters after the switch trains with all its capacity. The equilibrium is verified numerically on a grid of demand levels and arrival rates; I do not establish uniqueness or solve the symmetric equilibrium in mixed strategies.

Second, I identify *faith-based survival*, a channel from beliefs to solvency that runs through the allocation. Installed capacity carries a perpetual operating cost, so the firm's owners stop operating at a boundary that exists without any debt and that leverage shifts. A higher arrival rate raises the weight on the post-AGI continuation value and, when the firm trains enough, lowers that boundary. I characterize the threshold on the training fraction in closed form for a single-boundary reduction of the default problem (Proposition 2), and the optimal allocation exceeds it for arrival rates above about $0.034$ at baseline. At a fixed belief the boundary is U-shaped in the training fraction, so training beyond the optimum raises it. The continuation value is lost in default, yet a larger training fraction does not lower what creditors recover where the model's firms operate: recovery is at most $5\%$ of the claim at the model's policies and rises with the training fraction there, so credit risk is the risk of reaching the boundary, and the spread on debt issued at entry falls as the training fraction rises over the range examined (@sec-valuation).

Third, I quantify *Dario's dilemma*, the loss a firm incurs by investing on a belief about the AGI arrival rate $\lambda$ that differs from its true value (Numerical Finding 1). Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei describes the optimistic side: "I could buy \$1 trillion of compute that starts at the end of 2027... there's no hedge on Earth that could stop me from going bankrupt" [@amodei2026dwarkesh]. A mistaken belief changes the date, the scale, and the training allocation of the investment, and the allocation is the largest component of the loss on both sides. For a single firm with precommitted post-switch scale, with values measured at half the informed firm's trigger, investing as though $\lambda = 0.02$ when the true rate is $0.10$ costs $32\%$ of firm value, against $1.3\%$ for investing as though $\lambda = 0.18$, an error of the same size in $\lambda$. The comparison depends on how the two errors are matched. For equal proportional errors the pessimistic error still costs more, by a smaller factor ($32\%$ against $13\%$ at a factor of five, $\lambda = 0.02$ and $0.50$), and for equal errors in the expected time to the switch the ranking reverses ($1.0\%$ against $1.3\%$ at $4.4$ years). The pessimistic firm does not invest late in this problem: it invests early and small, with too little training. Tail risk comes from operating costs more than from debt. Each mistaken firm enters closer than the informed firm to the boundary at which it stops operating, and the far optimist ($\lambda = 0.50$) reaches it within five years with probability $1.8\%$ without any debt, about eleven times the informed firm's $0.16\%$, and $4.3\%$ against $0.47\%$ at leverage $\ell = 0.40$ under fairly priced debt (no-switch upper bounds). In the duopoly a mistaken leader loses more on both sides, $48\%$, $1.7\%$ and $32\%$ at the same three beliefs. A stylized calibration maps the training allocations assigned to four AI lab archetypes into implied beliefs and carries them through these objects (@sec-calibration); because the allocations are assigned, the exercise shows what they would imply and is not evidence that beliefs explain differences across firms.

{{< include _literature.qmd >}}

The paper proceeds as follows. @sec-model presents the environment, the single-firm benchmark, and the duopoly entry game with default risk, and contains Propositions 1 to 3. @sec-calibration describes the stylized calibration to frontier AI lab archetypes. @sec-valuation reports the quantitative implications: the allocation thresholds, Dario's dilemma, and credit risk at the model's policies. @sec-discussion considers testable predictions, policy implications, and limitations, and @sec-conclusion concludes. The Internet Appendix collects the proofs, numerical verification methods, calibration sources, robustness exercises, and supporting figures.
